opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think anyone has a settled answer yet. Right now we're in this odd place where most people interact with these models through raw strings: you write a prompt, you concatenate some text, you parse whatever comes back with a regex and hope for the best. That feels a lot like where we were with neural networks before autodiff frameworks, when everyone was hand-deriving gradients and gluing things together in ad hoc ways.

So my instinct, coming from the deep learning world, is that we want something that sits a level above the string. You'd like to think of a language model call as a function with some structure: it takes typed inputs, produces typed or at least constrained outputs, and can be composed with other calls and with ordinary code. That's the idea behind a lot of the work I've been interested in, things like MiniChain and the broader family of prompt-chaining libraries. The goal isn't to hide the prompt. I actually think hiding the prompt too aggressively is a mistake, because the prompt is where a lot of the real engineering happens. The goal is to make the prompt a visible, inspectable object that lives inside a program you can reason about.

At the same time, I'm a bit skeptical of building really heavy abstractions too early. Some of the frameworks out there have dozens of classes for agents and memories and tools, and when the underlying models change every six months, those abstractions tend to leak or become obsolete. It's a little like building an elaborate compiler for a hardware target that keeps changing under you.

So if I had to put a pin in it, I'd say the right level today is pretty thin: treat model calls as functions, keep prompts as first-class, readable templates, make the data flow between calls explicit so you can visualize and debug it, and lean on constrained generation, grammars, schemas, so the outputs plug cleanly into the rest of your code. Then, as we learn which patterns actually recur, we can grow higher-level abstractions out of those, rather than guessing at them up front. In a way it's the same lesson we learned with PyTorch: give people simple, composable primitives that stay close to what's really happening, and let the higher-level stuff emerge from practice.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually the central question right now, and I don't think we've settled it. Let me give you my honest take, which is that we keep oscillating between two extremes and the right answer is probably somewhere uncomfortable in the middle.

On one end you have the "just write a prompt" view. The model is the program. You describe what you want in English, maybe you give a few examples, and you're done. The appeal is obvious. It's incredibly fast to iterate, and it's accessible to people who aren't programmers at all. The problem is that it doesn't compose. The moment you want to chain two things together, or handle a failure case, or do something a thousand times with slightly different inputs, you're back to writing code anyway, except now you're writing code around a black box that behaves differently every time you touch the wording.

On the other end you have the people who want to treat the LM as a pure function and build full programming-language-style abstractions on top. Typed inputs, typed outputs, a compiler that optimizes your prompts, and so on. I'm sympathetic to that, and I've worked on things in that spirit. But I think it can over-claim. The model isn't actually a deterministic function. The types are soft. And there's a real risk of building a very elegant tower on top of something that fundamentally doesn't respect the abstraction.

So where do I land? I think the useful level right now looks something like what we had in the early days of neural nets, before the big frameworks fully matured. You want a thin layer that gives you a couple of things. First, structure: a clean way to say "this is a call to the model, here are its inputs, here's what shape I expect back." Second, control flow that lives in a real language, not in the prompt. Loops, branching, retries, those belong in Python or whatever you're using, not in a paragraph of natural language that the model may or may not follow. And third, and I think this is the underappreciated one, some notion of a signature or a declarative specification that's separate from the exact string you send to the model. Because the exact string is going to change. The model is going to change. If your whole system is tied to a specific phrasing that worked on one checkpoint, you've written something extremely brittle.

The analogy I keep coming back to is autodiff. Before autodiff, people wrote gradients by hand and it was error-prone and nobody wanted to touch it. The abstraction that won wasn't the highest-level one, it was the one that let you write ordinary code and then handled the annoying mechanical part for you. I think the equivalent for LMs is something that lets you write ordinary programs where some of the functions happen to be fuzzy, and then handles things like prompt formatting, output parsing, and maybe eventually prompt optimization behind the scenes.

Where I'd push back on my own field a bit is that we tend to want to jump straight to the grand unified framework. I think we're still in a phase where the right move is to keep the abstractions small and let people see what's underneath. If a developer can't look at the actual prompt being sent and the actual string coming back, they're going to have a very bad time debugging. So whatever level we pick, it needs to be transparent in a way that a lot of current tooling isn't.

The last thing I'd say is that the honest answer depends on who's programming. For a researcher who wants to try fifty variants of an idea in an afternoon, lower-level and closer to the raw prompt is better. For someone building a product that has to work for a year, you want more structure and more separation between intent and implementation. We probably need both, and we should stop pretending one abstraction is going to serve everyone.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s still a pretty open question. One way to program with a language model is to treat it as a function: you put a string in, you get a string out, and you write your program around that. That’s a very useful abstraction, but it hides some of the things that make these models interesting. You have a distribution over possible continuations, and you can potentially constrain or guide that distribution.

So I’m interested in an interface where you can mix ordinary programming with generation. If you know that something has to follow a particular structure, you should be able to express that directly. Then you let the model handle the parts where you actually need its ability to interpret language or generalize.

The challenge is figuring out how much of that machinery to expose. You don’t want every application developer to become an expert in decoding, but you do want them to have more control than just asking the model politely to return the right format. I think there’s a lot of room between those two extremes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s still a pretty open question. One extreme is that you just write everything in natural language, and the model figures out what you mean. The other is that you keep programming the way you do now and treat the model as a function you call. My intuition is that there’s an interesting space in between those two.

You want to be able to say, “Here’s the task,” and let the model handle the parts where language and ambiguity are useful. But you also want ordinary programming constructs for things you actually know: constraints, control flow, how to check the result. It seems strange to describe a constraint in a paragraph and then hope the model follows it when you could just enforce it in code.

So I’m interested in abstractions that let those two things interact cleanly. What can you delegate to the model, and what should the programming system guarantee? I don’t think we’ve found the right interface yet.
